text:
To the reeve and the good people of Ashford, greeting. We have heard your complaint about the mill and we answer it here, so that the matter may rest until the next court.

The miller shall grind the grain of every household in turn, beginning with the poorest, and he shall take no more than the sixteenth part as his fee. Whoever brings wet grain shall wait until the dry has been ground, and no one shall carry flour away before the measure has been checked by two neighbours chosen at the spring meeting. Let this be read at the church door on three Sundays.

Written in haste at the priory gate, with our seal pressed below, and sent by the hand of the carrier who knows the road.

To the warden of the bridge at Ashford, greeting. The spring floods have carried away two of the timbers, and the carters complain that the road is closed to them.

Every man who keeps a cart shall give one day of work each summer to the repair of the bridge over the river, bringing his own tools and food, and the warden shall write down the names of those who come and of those who send excuses, so that the account may be read aloud at the autumn court. We ask you to begin before the hay harvest.

Written in haste at the priory gate, with our seal pressed below, and sent by the hand of the carrier who knows the road.

To our brother at the cell of Little Brook. The sheep that were lent to you last winter are to be returned before shearing, with any lambs they have borne, and the shepherd is to be paid from your own stores.

We have sent a cask of salt and a bolt of grey cloth, which you will divide among the lay servants as you see fit.

Written in haste at the priory gate, with our seal pressed below, and sent by the hand of the carrier who knows the road.

A copy of the old order about the mill, written again for the new miller, who says he never saw it.

The myller shall grinde the grain of every houshold in turne, begynning with the poorest, and he shall take no more than the sixtenth part as his fee. Whoever bringeth wet grain shall wait until the dry hath been ground, and no one shall carry flour away before the measure hath been checked by two neighbours chosen at the spring meeting. Copied faithfully from the roll kept in the chest.

Let the new miller swear to keep it before the steward and two witnesses.

To the reeve of Ashford. The lord bishop will pass through your village on his way to the coast, and he is to be given bread, ale and fodder for twelve horses.

No market shall be held that day, and the road by the green is to be cleared of carts and pens.

Written in haste at the priory gate, with our seal pressed below, and sent by the hand of the carrier who knows the road.

Concerning the bridge, as it was ordered in the time of the old prior, with a word added for the people beyond the marsh.

Every man who keeps a cart shall give one day of work each summer to the repair of the bridge over the river, bringing his own tools and food. Those who live beyond the marsh are excused in years of flood. And the warden shall write down the names of those who come and of those who send excuses, so that the account may be read aloud at the autumn court.

The warden is to bring the account to the steward when it has been read.

At the autumn court the miller was accused of taking a larger share of the grain than is allowed.

The jurors recalled that he shall take no more than the sixteenth part as his fee. Whoever brings wet grain shall wait until the dry has been ground, and they found that he had taken a twelfth part in the dry months. He was fined and warned.

The next court will be held after the feast of Saint Martin.

To the reeve of Ashford. We have received the fine from the autumn court and the account of the bridge.

The warden has done well, and he may keep the old timbers for his own use.

Written in haste at the priory gate, with our seal pressed below, and sent by the hand of the carrier who knows the road.
